headline: Monday opened quiet on the fears and loud on the data: the Iran deal didn't sign and Beirut didn't answer — crude's Sunday open came flat and the haven bid stayed sheathed. Instead the market got a two-track China beat (GDP 4.5%, retail sales the surprise at +1.1%) that made the aussie the night's best G10 performer, a hawkish RBA Kent questioning whether policy is 'restrictive enough,' and violent French protests that gave the euro its first real negative driver in days. This morning is Canada CPI at 7:30am CT — October-28 hike odds sit at just ~25-32%, and only a hot print revives them.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: Monday opened on neither of Sunday's fears: no signed Iran deal (talks stalled), no Hezbollah retaliation (decision pending) — crude's Sunday open came flat and the haven bid stayed sheathed. DXY 101.80-101.83 in Asia, flat; October stays a hold (~84-87%) into the Oct 17-29 blackout. China's 4.5% GDP beat firmed the yuan (USD/CNH 6.6811, strongest since June 2022) but barely moved the dollar elsewhere.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Sunday's two binary risks both resolved as continuations. First, the signing test failed again — FM Araqchi said Sunday that Tehran's seven-day Hormuz-reopening offer is 'still on the table' but negotiations have stalled, with a sequencing deadlock (Washington wants enrichment addressed first; Tehran wants maritime security first). Trump's 'complete' claim is now two days old with no ceremony, no text, no Iranian confirmation. Second, Hezbollah has not answered Sunday's Beirut strike: official Mahmoud Qmati said it crossed a 'red line' and leadership will decide if/how to respond, the IRGC said the 'right to avenge' is preserved — but Hezbollah itself issued no retaliation threat, and the IDF told northern-Israel residents to continue normal routines, signaling no response is expected. The four-beat read on the failed signing: (1) a US-Iran deal remains a claim, not a document; (2) the surprise, if any, is how thoroughly the claim has aged without confirmation — two days of 'complete' with zero corroboration is itself information; (3) against the benchmark of June, when the same narrative collapsed, an unconfirmed claim is a headline, not a deflation event — and the deflation a real signing would bring stays unpriced; (4) for the dollar this keeps the weekend's soft-dollar read intact: the haven leg never got its bid and the relief leg never got its deal. The one-question lens: is anything actually signed, or is this another claim week? Crude's Sunday open (~5pm CT) priced the answer first — Brent ~$109.9, WTI ~$101.4 indicative, flat on the week — and by Asia Monday Brent slipped 1.0-1.8% (~$108) while WTI held ~$101. The rate thesis is untouched: the Fed is silent in the blackout (Oct 17-29), October priced as a hold at ~84-87%, December the debate (~89.5%, but that figure is Oct-15 vintage — flagged). Thread: Friday closed the week soft-dollar — DXY 101.61, first weekly loss in five, on the October-hike fade; Sunday added claim day and escalation day; Monday opened with neither one firing. What it means: confirms — the soft-dollar weekend thesis holds, but nothing extended it. The dollar's next move waits on data, not geopolitics: today's Canada CPI (for the CAD leg), then the week's CPI cluster — UK Wednesday, NZ Wednesday — and US housing Tuesday before the blackout ends at the Oct 27-28 FOMC.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro got its first real negative driver in days: violent cost-of-living protests in France — Macron's Sunday address condemned 'shocking' scenes — pushed EUR/USD -0.1% to ~1.1225 at the Asia open and the OAT-Bund spread to ~140bp. Until budget clarity, rallies are expected to be sold. France's revenue vote is Tuesday; Moody's is Friday.
chapters.meaning: What changed: an actual euro-driver arrived, and it's negative. Saturday's cost-of-living protests were described as one of France's worst days of unrest in years, and Macron's televised Sunday address condemning 'shocking' scenes confirmed the state of play. EUR/USD fell 0.1% to ~1.1225-1.1230 at the Asia open, dropped below 1.12 at the Sunday open, and fell broadly — EUR/JPY below 177, EUR/CHF below 0.9250 at the Sunday open. The four-beat read on the spread: (1) the OAT-Bund spread is the extra yield investors demand to hold French government bonds over Germany's — the market's real-time verdict on French fiscal credibility; (2) it sits near 140bp, wider than last week's ~135bp; (3) against the benchmark of the ECB's wait for December, a wider French spread is the euro's domestic headwind getting heavier, not lighter — and it moves independently of anything the Fed does; (4) for the euro the transmission is bonds, not the street: as InTouch's Kieran Williams put it, the unrest matters 'mainly through French bonds rather than directly' — 'appetite for the euro is likely to stay thin this week and I'd expect rallies to be sold until there is a clearer outcome on the budget.' The one-question lens: does France's budget fight get clearer or uglier this week? Thread: Friday's edition said the two-day rebound ran on dollar weakness, not euro strength — borrowed momentum — and the ECB leg is December (100% priced; October 29 is not a hike, with a Reuters poll of 70 of 73 economists expecting a hold at 2.50%). What it means: breaks the rebound thesis — the pair had been trading the Fed leg; it now has its own negative leg, and the budget calendar is the weight.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: No move in the pound (1.3329, flat) but a real expectations upgrade behind it: September CPI consensus hardened to 3.4% y/y vs 3.1% prior — Deutsche Bank sees 3.49% — and the Nov 5 hike is ~95% priced. The hinge is Wednesday 1am CT; Tuesday's labor dump (earnings 3.8% fc) comes first.
chapters.meaning: What changed: two small deltas. First, the market's expectation for Wednesday's UK CPI moved up: headline consensus is now 3.4% y/y (prev 3.1%, nine-month high) with Deutsche Bank at 3.49%, core 2.7% (prev 2.6%). The four-beat read: (1) headline inflation is expected at 3.4% for September, up from 3.1% in August; (2) against that consensus, a print at 3.5%+ is the surprise that reopens a December follow-up debate; (3) against the BoE's 2% target, 3.4% is still ~1.4 points hot — inflation running too hot, not cooling; (4) for sterling, hot cements the Nov 5 hike (~95% priced per market sources) and puts December on the table, while soft reopens Bailey's dovish 2027 read. Second, the Rightmove print was soft at the edges: asking prices +1.0% m/m in October (below the 1.3% seasonal average), -0.1% y/y, with 2-year fixed mortgage rates at 5.55% biting — low-tier, no FX read, but it confirms the rate-pressure texture under the GDP beat. Thread: Friday's edition said sterling's bid was the week's cleanest — GDP +0.1% vs -0.1% (2.1% y/y, strongest since Aug 2022) plus a priced November hike plus the dollar fade; Bailey's dovish lean is 2027-dated. What it means: confirms — the November case got firmer overnight, not softer. The question is no longer whether November happens but whether Wednesday's CPI is hot enough to start pricing December.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: Ueda's clearest hawkish phrase yet — underlying inflation 'quite close' to the 2% target — firms the December hike case (~80% OIS) without changing October (~25%). USD/JPY 158.00-158.08 in Asia, still pinned by the ~216bp US-Japan 10-year gap; 160 is the intervention line. Japan CPI prints Friday.
chapters.meaning: What changed: two small deltas. First, Ueda told parliament Monday that underlying inflation is 'quite close' to the 2% target — the four-beat read: (1) underlying inflation is the BoJ's preferred gauge, the one it watches rather than headline noise; (2) 'quite close' is the closest Ueda has come to declaring the precondition met; (3) against a 2% target, that's the setup for more hikes — but not a commitment, and words don't close a ~216bp yield gap, rate moves do; (4) for the yen, it firms December (~80% OIS) while leaving Oct 30 at ~25% — the yen's self-powered catalyst stays the Oct 29-30 meeting, where fresh quarterly forecasts publish the pace signal. Second, Japan's August tertiary activity fell 0.1% m/m — a beat vs -0.3% expected, though the first decline in two months — leaving services recovering, not rolling. USD/JPY traded 158.00-158.08 in Asia (Tokyo range 157.70-158.11), flat, confirming the laggard read: the dollar faded, the yen didn't follow. Thread: Friday's edition said the yen needs the US 10-year to fall, not just the dollar — Ueda's lean stands but the market prices December. What it means: confirms — Ueda's words got sharper but the structure is unchanged: the yen is a yield-gap trade into the BoJ, with 160 the line Tokyo watches.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The night's double delta: China's Q3 GDP beat 4.5% (retail sales the standout at +1.1% vs 0.5-0.6% fc) made the aussie the best G10 performer (+0.3-0.5% to ~0.6965-0.6977), and RBA Kent questioned whether a 4.60% cash rate is 'restrictive enough' — keeping a Nov 2-3 hike on the table. But the rally still looks rented: funds sit long AUD at the 79th percentile, so the pain trade is down.
chapters.meaning: What changed: two real deltas. First, the GDP beat: (1) China's economy grew 4.5% y/y in Q3 vs 4.4% expected, q/q 1.2% vs ~1.0-1.1%, YTD 4.6% — on track for the ~5% annual target; (2) the texture is the story — September retail sales +1.1% y/y vs 0.5-0.6% forecast (2x expectations, up from 0.4%), while fixed-asset investment ran -7.2% and property investment is -20.6% YTD; (3) against the target, China is keeping pace — but the beat is factory/export-led (industrial output +5.5%), not domestic, with the NBS itself flagging weak domestic demand; (4) for the aussie: China is Australia's biggest customer, and export-led growth bids iron ore and the currency — the 4.5% print is mildly positive, the property drag is the cap. The market's read confirmed it: AUD held ~0.6970 through the Asia open with no extension of the GDP pop — priced and moved on. Second, Kent: (1) he said there's 'reasonable evidence' neutral rates are rising in Australia and globally — a 4.60% cash rate may be exerting less restraint than it looks; (2) the surprise is the openness: he questioned whether policy is 'restrictive enough' and called the market's post-jobs-report trimming of hike odds 'sensible'; (3) against a 4.7% unemployment rate (five-year high) and underlying inflation stuck at 3.6% for three straight months, the RBA faces a hard trade-off — looser labor vs sticky inflation; (4) for the aussie: November stays live (~30% priced, December ~50%), with Q3 CPI on Oct 28 the pivot. Thread: Friday's edition said the positioning lens flipped — funds long AUD at the 79th percentile, which broke the squeeze story; under the contrarian rule, stretched longs mean the pain trade is down, not up. What it means: the two deltas pull opposite ways — the fundamentals (China beat + Kent's hawkish lean) firm the aussie's floor, but the positioning overhang says Friday's and tonight's rallies are rented, not owned. The one-question lens: if risk wobbles, who gets carried out first — the most crowded long?

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: CPI day: 7:30am CT brings the September print — TD 3.2%, UBS 3.3%, RBC 3.0% (vs 3.0% prior) — and a pricing reality check: October-28 hike odds sit at just ~25-32% after the -68.3K jobs miss, not the coin flip the weekend read implied. Only a hot print (3.3%+) revives October; soft buries it to December. USD/CAD 1.4122 in Asia, ~flat.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the calendar's biggest domestic binary. The four-beat read on the CPI setup: (1) September headline inflation is expected around 3.2% (TD) to 3.3% (UBS), vs 3.0% in August, with core trim/median near 1.9% and common at 2.6% (FF); (2) the surprise band is wide — 3.3%+ is hot, 3.0% or below is soft, and the three bank forecasts span it; (3) against the BoC's 2% target, 3.2% is well above — but the economy that produced it is loosening: -68.3K September jobs, unemployment 6.5% (vs 6.4%), participation at a 29-year low (64.8%) — headline heat vs labor slack, the classic central-bank fork; (4) for the loonie: hot → October hike repriced from ~27% toward 50%+, USD/CAD tests 1.40; soft → October dead, the hike becomes December's (~88%), USD/CAD back over 1.42. Thread: Friday's edition had Macklem's hawkish lean ('harder to look through' energy prices) putting October back on the table — but the pricing check says the market never bought it: LSEG 25%, TD 27%, rateprobability 32% as of Oct 18. What it means: challenges the weekend thesis — the jobs tape beat Macklem, and only a hot CPI re-arms him. Second, the oil leg is neutral at the open: Sunday's reopen came flat and WTI held ~$101 into Asia, so the loonie has no crude tailwind to lean on. The BoC's own business survey lands at 10:30am CT, framing the Oct 28 decision alongside CPI.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: Small but real deltas: the September trade deficit blew out to NZ$1.97B vs 0.78B fc (fuel imports +96% y/y, price-driven), and services PSI cooled to 50.9 — both feed the RBNZ's hold side mildly. NZD/USD 0.5655-0.5661, flat in Asia. Wednesday's Q3 CPI (4:45pm CT, ANZ 3.8% y/y) still decides the Oct 28 two-way bet.
chapters.meaning: What changed: the trade print. The four-beat read: (1) New Zealand imported NZ$8.44B and exported NZ$6.47B in September, leaving a NZ$1.97B deficit vs 0.78B expected — exports actually rose 12% y/y (dairy, meat), imports surged 18% on a +96% y/y fuel bill; (2) the surprise is mostly price, not volume — crude prices did the damage, plus a one-off aircraft purchase; (3) against the RBNZ's framework, a wide deficit is a soft-demand signal but a fuel-price-driven one is a supply shock — they pull opposite ways, so this is texture, not a pivot; (4) for the kiwi: a mild drag heading into Oct 28, but Wednesday's CPI is the settler. Services PSI cooled to 50.9 (from 51.2) — fourth month of expansion, losing momentum, the same soft-domestic-demand picture as the flat food prices. Thread: Friday's edition had the two-way bet — the 56.5 PMI (strongest since 2021, 15th straight expansion) feeds the hike side, flat food prices feed the hold side, Conway calls Oct 28 'wide open' with direction 'most likely up'. What it means: confirms — the two-way bet is intact; the trade and services prints tilt it a fraction toward the hold side, but ANZ's 3.8% (vs 4.1% Q2, vs RBNZ's own 3.9% projection) is the number that actually decides. The one-question lens: does Q3 CPI come in hot enough to justify 'most likely up'?

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Assessment Monday: the Sunday reopen came flat (Brent ~$109.9 / WTI ~$101.4) — neither the deal-tumble nor the escalation spike. Asia took Brent -1.0 to -1.8% (~$108), WTI held ~$101. Petersburg's terminal fire is confirmed (FP-1 strike, ~1 killed) but the damage is unquantified; the Hormuz mine claim is still unconfirmed; no signed deal; no Hezbollah retaliation. The spread ~$7.5-8 still reads as tanker-risk premium at ~2x normal.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Monday is assessment day, and the assessments split. First, the price read: crude's Sunday open came flat — the market priced neither a signed deal (the deflation leg) nor new escalation (the premium leg); by Asia Monday Brent slipped 1.0-1.8% (~$108.0-108.8) while WTI held ~$100.8-101.2, which reads as mild relief on the Russia side (the waiver easing supply fears) rather than Hormuz confidence. The four-beat read on the spread: (1) Brent trades ~$7.5-8 over WTI; (2) normal is ~$3-5 — the premium is roughly double; (3) a wide spread is the market's price for tanker risk, not demand: it's what the world pays to move crude through dangerous water over the US benchmark; (4) for FX it stays the CAD-vs-importers tell in one number — wide favors CAD, collapse hurts it. Second, Petersburg: the terminal fire is confirmed — Governor Beglov reported the strike, Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point confirmed its FP-1 hit the terminal, Pulkovo restricted, roughly 1 killed and several injured (figures vary across sources) — but no throughput-loss figure exists; the terminal moves 12.5M tonnes a year and any operational impact is still unassessed. Third, the signing test failed again: no deal, talks stalled, the 7-day Hormuz offer 'still on the table' — and Tehran's sequencing deadlock with Washington (enrichment first vs maritime first) hasn't moved. Fourth, the mine claim stays unconfirmed: Reuters and a second wire carry the IRGC statement — two tankers, ~2M barrels each — but no ship names, no independent verification; Kpler puts Hormuz crude transit at 2.9M bpd (Oct 11) vs 20.8M (Oct 8). Held, not priced. Thread: Saturday's ledger was the record attack week (12 vessels, RPG-from-small-boat as a new attack type), the IRGC's 'closed' vs Cooper's 'controlled by the United States'; Sunday became claim day; Monday is the market's verdict so far — continuity. What it means: the war premium now runs on two live engines — Hormuz (claims, still unpriced) and escalation (Beirut, freshly open but not yet answered). The waiver stands with bipartisan backlash but no reversal — the duties channel stays deflated.

chapters.teaser: Quiet: spot $4,175-4,198 (+0.2-0.4%) in Asia — the anti-dollar bid held but still didn't extend, capped below $4,200 by December-hike pricing (~89.5%, Oct-15 vintage). The cap breaks only if December pricing cracks or a real escalation re-arms the haven bid.
chapters.meaning: What changed: nothing since Friday's close — gold pushed toward $4,200 intraday and faded. Thread: Friday's edition said gold is doing exactly what the framework says — up on dollar weakness and falling yields (10-year ~5.07-5.10%), capped by hot US inflation prints and a priced December hike; still ~23% below January's $5,405 record. What it means: thesis stands — gold's message is the dollar's message in reverse. Neither of Sunday's risks re-armed the haven leg at the open, so the cap holds. What would change it: a crack in December-hike pricing lifts the cap ($4,217-4,262 opens); a real escalation re-arms the haven bid; hot headlines push it back under $4,150.
